entries.summary: Mahavira (also known as Vardhamana) is the 24th and last Tirthankara of the current cosmic cycle. Traditional accounts place his birth in 599 BCE (Śvētāmbara) or 615 BCE (Digambara) in Vaishali (present-day Bihar, India) into a royal Kshatriya family. At around age 30, he renounced his royal life, family, and possessions to seek spiritual liberation. After approximately 12.5 years of rigorous ascetic practice, he attained Kevala Jnana (omniscience). He spent the remaining ~30 years teaching the Jain path. He attained nirvana (liberation) at Pavapuri. His nirvana day is celebrated as Jain Diwali.
entries.tradition_notes: Digambara and Śvētāmbara traditions share the core narrative of Mahavira's life but differ on some biographical details. Key differences noted below.

entries.summary: Traditional accounts say Mahavira was born to King Siddhartha and Queen Trishala in Kundagrama (near Vaishali). His birth was accompanied by auspicious dreams. He grew up as a prince in comfort. Traditional accounts describe him marrying Yashoda and having a daughter, Priyadarshana. Around age 30 (after his parents passed away by Sallekhana in Digambara accounts, or at the appropriate time in Śvētāmbara accounts), he renounced all possessions and began his ascetic life.
entries.tradition_notes: Digambara tradition: Mahavira never married; he renounced worldly life before marriage. Śvētāmbara tradition: Mahavira married Yashoda and had a daughter, Priyadarshana, before renouncing. This is one of the well-known biographical differences between the two traditions.

entries.summary: After renunciation, Mahavira practiced intense austerities for approximately 12.5 years. He observed complete silence, tolerated hardships without complaint, and moved from place to place practicing non-violence scrupulously. He pulled out his hair (kesh lochan) as part of his renunciation. This period is described in Jain texts as an extraordinary demonstration of endurance and spiritual discipline.
entries.tradition_notes: Digambara: Mahavira renounced even clothing (went sky-clad) from the moment of renunciation. Śvētāmbara: He initially wore a robe given by a Deva (celestial being), which he discarded after 13 months.

entries.summary: After approximately 12.5 years of ascetic practice, Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana — complete, perfect, infinite knowledge of all things past, present, and future — while meditating under a sal tree near the banks of the Rijupalika river. At this point he became a Jina (conqueror of inner enemies) and a Sarvagna (omniscient). He then began teaching (deshana) to his followers.
entries.tradition_notes: Both traditions agree on the attainment of Kevala Jnana. Specific location details vary slightly in textual accounts.

entries.summary: After attaining Kevala Jnana, Mahavira organized a fourfold Sangha (community): monks (sadhus), nuns (sadhvis), laymen (shravakas), and laywomen (shravikas). He had 11 chief disciples called Ganadharas, of whom Indrabhuti Gautama is the most well-known. Mahavira's teachings are preserved in the Jain Agamas (Śvētāmbara) and other texts.
entries.tradition_notes: Digambara tradition holds that the original Agamas were lost after Mahavira's nirvana. Śvētāmbara tradition holds that the Agamas were preserved, though in modified form.

entries.summary: Mahavira attained nirvana (liberation) at Pavapuri, Bihar, traditionally dated to 527 BCE (Śvētāmbara) or 515 BCE (Digambara). The night of his nirvana is celebrated as Jain Diwali (Dipa Purnima or Vira Nirvana Samvat), when Jains light lamps to mark the passing of the 'lamp of knowledge' from the world. Pavapuri is one of the holiest pilgrimage sites for Jains.
entries.tradition_notes: Both traditions celebrate Mahavira Nirvana Diwali, though dates may differ slightly based on their respective calendars.
